---
title: "Week 2 Exercises - Files, Pipes, and First Shell Scripts"
---

Short, **ungraded** practice tasks - about 30-40 minutes. Companion reading: [Ch. 6](../book/chapters/06-unix-environment.html) and [Ch. 7](../book/chapters/07-files-pipes.html), with [Ch. 5](../book/chapters/05-unix-fundamentals.html) as review.

## Files, directories, and pipes

1.  Inside `~/projects/comptools`, build a project skeleton in one command: `mkdir -p data/raw data/processed scripts output/figures output/tables docs` - the structure from Lecture 01.
2.  Run `ls -F` and confirm the directories are there (the `/` suffix marks directories).
3.  Create a `README.md` with `nano`: type one sentence describing the project, save (`Ctrl+O`, Enter), and exit (`Ctrl+X`). Print it with `cat`.
4.  Download the course dataset into `data/raw` (the command is on the L02 slides and in [Ch. 1](../book/chapters/01-introduction.html#sec-course-dataset)). If you already downloaded it, `cp` or `mv` it into `data/raw`.
5.  How many lines does `Stickle_RNAseq.tsv` have (`wc -l`)? Given 80 fish, why that number?
6.  Look at just the first three lines with `head -n 3`. Too wide to read? Try `cut -f1-4 data/raw/Stickle_RNAseq.tsv | head -n 3` to see only the first four columns.
7.  In a scratch directory, create `file_1.txt`, `file_2.txt`, and `file_3.txt` with one `touch` command, then list them with the wildcard `file_?.txt`.
8.  Save a directory listing to a file with redirection: `ls -lh data/raw > output/data_inventory.txt`, then `cat` it.

## Shell scripts and permissions

9.  In `scripts/`, use `nano` to create `hello.sh` containing the two lines from the L02 slides (the `#!/usr/bin/env bash` shebang and an `echo`). Try `./hello.sh` - read the error out loud.
10. Run `ls -l hello.sh` and decode the ten-character permission string: who can read it? Write it? Run it?
11. Fix it with `chmod u+x hello.sh`, check `ls -l` again to see what changed, and run it. Then try `bash hello.sh` - why does that work even without `x`?
12. Download the four example scripts from the [Example Files page](../Examples.html) into `scripts/` and make them all executable with one command: `chmod +x *.sh`.
13. Run `./file_inventory.sh ~/projects/comptools inventory.txt` and open the report. Which file type takes the most space in your project?
14. Try the two-script pipeline on the dataset: `./filter_rows.sh Genotype A < ../data/raw/Stickle_RNAseq.tsv | ./total_counts.sh | sort -t$'\t' -k2,2nr | head -5`. Which fish has the most reads? Rerun for genotype B.
15. Scripts are just text, so modify one and run it again: open `total_counts.sh` in `nano`, change the header it prints from `Total_counts` to `Total_reads`, save, and rerun the pipeline from the previous task. Two things to notice: your change shows up immediately, and no new `chmod` was needed - the execute permission belongs to the file, not to its contents.
16. Make a dated snapshot of your whole project: `cd ~/projects && comptools/scripts/backup_project.sh comptools`. List the archive's contents with `tar -tzf <archive-name>` - your `output/` folder should be missing while everything else is there. Read the script's comments to see why `output/` is treated as expendable.
17. Protect your raw data the Unix way: `chmod a-w data/raw/*`, then try `echo "oops" >> data/raw/Stickle_RNAseq.tsv` and watch the shell refuse. (Undo later with `chmod u+w` if you ever need to - but should you?)

Done early? Run `./make_project.sh practice_project` and compare its layout to the skeleton you built by hand in task 1, then read the script's comments to see how it works.
